entities.summary:
Johannes Stöffler was a German mathematician, astronomer, astrologer, priest, maker of astronomical instruments and professor at the University of Tübingen.

Born in 1452 in Blaubeuren, Swabia, Stöffler studied at the University of Tübingen, where he received his doctorate in 1476.

He became a professor of mathematics and astronomy at the University of Tübingen in 1480 and served in various capacities for the Holy Roman Emperor, including as a member of the Imperial Chamber Court.

Stöffler was a prolific writer and published numerous works on mathematics, astronomy, and astrology, including the widely used astronomical table known as the Stöffler-Nepveu Table.

Stöffler's work had a significant impact on the development of astronomy in Europe during the Renaissance, and he is considered one of the most important mathematicians and astronomers of his time.

Despite his significant contributions, Stöffler's life was not without controversy, as he was involved in a famous astronomical dispute with the astronomer Johann Müller von Konigsberg.

Stöffler died in 1531 in Tübingen, leaving behind a legacy as one of the most important mathematicians and astronomers of the Renaissance.

Stöffler's work continued to influence the development of astronomy and mathematics for centuries after his death, and he remains a celebrated figure in the history of science.

In 1988, Stöffler was posthumously awarded the prestigious Copley Medal by the Royal Society for his outstanding contributions to the field of astronomy.

Stöffler's work has been recognized for its significance in the development of astronomy and mathematics, and he is widely regarded as one of the most important figures in the history of science.

The University of Tübingen still maintains a museum dedicated to Stöffler's life and work, and his legacy continues to inspire mathematicians and astronomers around the world.
